explanation.exam_pattern: After-action / root-cause / improvements = Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned) -> feeds Preparation.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Incident response (post-incident activity)

questions.stem: An organization is maturing its incident-response preparation. Which TWO measures MOST improve readiness BEFORE an incident occurs? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep the only copy of the IR plan on a network share that ransomware could encrypt
Wait for a real incident to discover gaps in the process
Pre-establish roles, communication plans (including out-of-band channels), and retainer/legal/breach-notification contacts
Maintain tested IR playbooks and run regular tabletop/simulation exercises

explanation.correct: Readiness comes from tested playbooks plus exercises, and from pre-established roles, out-of-band communications, and pre-arranged legal / IR-retainer / notification contacts - so the team acts quickly and correctly under pressure.

distractors.A: Storing the only IR-plan copy where ransomware can encrypt it means it may be unavailable exactly when needed (keep offline copies).
distractors.B: Waiting for a real incident to find gaps is reactive and increases damage - the opposite of preparation.

explanation.exam_pattern: IR preparation = tested playbooks + exercises + defined roles/out-of-band comms + pre-arranged legal/notification contacts; keep offline copies.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Incident response (preparation, playbooks, communications)

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the acronym: The open framework that produces a standardized 0.0-10.0 severity score (using Base, Temporal/Threat, and Environmental metric groups) for a vulnerability is the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, abbreviated ______.

explanation.correct: CVSS provides a standardized severity score from 0.0 to 10.0 using Base, Temporal/Threat, and Environmental metric groups; it measures severity but should be combined with exploitability and asset context for true prioritization.
explanation.exam_pattern: Standardized 0-10 vulnerability severity = CVSS; severity alone is not risk - add exploitability + asset context.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Vulnerability management (CVSS)

questions.stem: A scanner reports 4,000 vulnerabilities, far more than the team can patch at once. Several are CVSS 9.8 but on isolated test systems with no exploit seen in the wild, while one CVSS 7.5 is on an internet-facing crown-jewel app and appears on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. Which prioritization approach is BEST?

options.text: Patch the oldest CVEs first regardless of context
Prioritize by risk: combine severity with real-world exploitability (e.g., EPSS, CISA KEV), asset exposure, and business criticality
Patch strictly in descending CVSS base-score order
Patch whatever is easiest to patch first

explanation.correct: Effective risk-based prioritization blends severity (CVSS) with exploitation likelihood (EPSS, CISA KEV / active exploitation), internet exposure, and business criticality - so the actively exploited, internet-facing crown-jewel issue outranks a high-CVSS flaw on an isolated test box.

distractors.A: The age of a CVE is not a sound risk signal by itself.
distractors.C: CVSS base score alone ignores exploitability and asset context, misranking real risk.
distractors.D: Ease of patching is operational convenience, not a measure of risk.

explanation.exam_pattern: Prioritize by risk = severity x exploitability (EPSS/KEV) x exposure x business impact, not CVSS alone.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Vulnerability management (risk-based prioritization, EPSS, CISA KEV)

questions.stem: A team's unauthenticated network scans keep missing patches and producing uncertainresults, because they can only see services from outside the host. Which change will MOST improve scan accuracy and reduce false positives for host configuration and patch state?

options.text: Only scan the perimeter firewall
Scan less frequently to reduce noise
Use authenticated (credentialed) scanning so the scanner can log in and inspect actual patch levels and configuration
Replace scanning with a one-time annual penetration test

explanation.correct: Credentialed (authenticated) scans log into hosts to read exact patch levels, configuration, and installed software, giving far more accurate results and fewer false positives than unauthenticated scans that only probe exposed services.

distractors.A: Scanning only the firewall ignores internal host state entirely.
distractors.B: Scanning less often reduces visibility and timeliness; it doesn't improve per-scan accuracy.
distractors.D: An annual pen test is point-in-time and doesn't replace continuous, accurate configuration/patch assessment.

explanation.exam_pattern: Accurate patch/config state + fewer false positives = authenticated (credentialed) scanning.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Vulnerability management (authenticated vs unauthenticated scanning)

questions.stem: A critical vulnerability is found in a legacy medical device that the vendor cannot patch for 9 months and that cannot be taken offline. Which response BEST manages the risk in the interim?

options.text: Apply compensating controls: isolate/segment the device, restrict access with ACLs/firewalls, add virtual patching/IPS, and increase monitoring until a patch is available
Formally accept the risk and take no technical action
Ignore it until the vendor releases a patch
Immediately disconnect the device regardless of patient impact

explanation.correct: When patching isn't feasible, compensating controls reduce exposure: network segmentation/isolation, strict access controls, virtual patching/IPS, and enhanced monitoring - managing the risk until the device can be remediated.

distractors.B: Formal acceptance with no mitigation leaves a known-critical risk unaddressed when controls are available.
distractors.C: Ignoring a critical, exploitable flaw for months leaves it fully exposed.
distractors.D: Disconnecting a device that cannot be taken offline may cause unacceptable safety/operational impact.

explanation.exam_pattern: Can't patch now -> compensating controls (segment, restrict, virtual-patch/IPS, monitor) until remediation.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Vulnerability management (compensating controls, risk mitigation)

questions.stem: A security team wants to aggregate logs from firewalls, servers, endpoints, and cloud, then correlate events across them to detect multi-stage attacks and alert in near real time. Which platform is designed for this?

options.text: A password manager
A load balancer
A vulnerability scanner
A SIEM (security information and event management)

explanation.correct: A SIEM centralizes and normalizes logs from many sources and applies correlation rules/analytics to detect multi-stage attacks and generate near-real-time alerts, serving as the SOC's analysis hub.

distractors.A: A password manager stores credentials, unrelated to event correlation.
distractors.B: A load balancer distributes traffic and is not a log-correlation/detection platform.
distractors.C: A vulnerability scanner finds weaknesses; it doesn't correlate live multi-source event logs.

explanation.exam_pattern: Aggregate + normalize + correlate multi-source logs with alerting = SIEM.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Monitoring/detection (SIEM, correlation)

questions.stem: A company wants to detect a compromised-but-valid account and a malicious insider by flagging deviations from each user's and device's normal behavior (e.g., unusual login times, data-access volumes, or locations), rather than by fixed signatures. Which capability BEST provides this?

options.text: User and entity behavior analytics (UEBA)
Signature-based IDS
A certificate revocation list (CRL)
A WAF

explanation.correct: UEBA builds behavioral baselines for users and entities and uses analytics/ML to flag anomalies (odd times, volumes, locations), making it well suited to detecting account compromise and insider threats that signatures miss.

distractors.B: A signature-based IDS matches known patterns and won't flag novel anomalous behavior by a valid account.
distractors.C: A CRL lists revoked certificates - unrelated to behavioral anomaly detection.
distractors.D: A WAF filters web-application attacks, not user-behavior anomalies across the enterprise.

explanation.exam_pattern: Baseline normal + flag anomalies for insiders/compromised accounts = UEBA (behavioral analytics).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Monitoring/detection (UEBA, anomaly detection)

questions.stem: An analyst correlating logs across firewalls, servers, and endpoints finds that timestamps disagree by minutes, making it impossible to reconstruct the true event sequence. Which foundational control MOST directly fixes this?

options.text: Reduce the number of log sources
Increase log retention to one year
Synchronize all systems to a common, reliable time source using NTP (with a consistent reference such as UTC)
Encrypt all log files at rest

explanation.correct: Accurate event correlation and timeline reconstruction require synchronized clocks; using NTP against a reliable source (and a consistent reference such as UTC) ensures timestamps line up across systems.

distractors.A: Fewer log sources reduces visibility and still wouldn't synchronize the remaining clocks.
distractors.B: Longer retention keeps logs available but does not align mismatched timestamps.
distractors.D: Encryption protects log confidentiality/integrity but does not synchronize clocks.

explanation.exam_pattern: Cross-source correlation/timelines depend on synchronized clocks = NTP (standardize on UTC).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Monitoring/detection (time synchronization, log correlation)

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: During evidence acquisition, the principle of collecting the most volatile data (such as CPU registers and RAM) before less volatile data (such as disk and archival media) is called the order of ______.

explanation.correct: The order of volatility (per RFC 3227) directs responders to capture the most ephemeral data first - registers/cache, then RAM, network state, disk, and finally archival media - so fragile evidence isn't lost.
explanation.exam_pattern: Collect most-ephemeral-first (registers/RAM -> disk -> archives) = order of volatility (RFC 3227).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Digital forensics (order of volatility)

questions.stem: For evidence to be admissible, an investigator must document every person who handled a piece of evidence, plus when and why, from collection all the way to court. Which concept is this?

options.text: Chain of custody
Order of volatility
Legal hold
Data remanence

explanation.correct: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who collected, handled, transferred, and stored evidence (and when and why), preserving its integrity and admissibility.

distractors.B: Order of volatility governs the sequence of data collection, not custody documentation.
distractors.C: A legal hold preserves potentially relevant data from deletion; it isn't the handling record for a specific exhibit.
distractors.D: Data remanence is residual data left after deletion, unrelated to custody tracking.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unbroken documented handling record for admissibility = chain of custody.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Digital forensics (chain of custody)

questions.stem: An analyst must forensically acquire a running server suspected of hosting only in-memory (fileless) malware, then image its disk. Which approach BEST preserves evidence integrity?

options.text: Reboot the server into the OS and run antivirus before imaging
Pull the power immediately, then image the disk, skipping memory
Capture volatile memory (RAM) from the live system first, then acquire a disk image using a write blocker and verify both with cryptographic hashes
Copy a few suspicious files out with normal OS tools and call it done

explanation.correct: Fileless malware lives in RAM, so capture volatile memory from the live system first; then image the disk through a write blocker and verify the images with cryptographic hashes to prove integrity. This respects the order of volatility and preserves admissibility.

distractors.A: Rebooting and running AV changes system state, destroys memory evidence, and can alter or delete artifacts.
distractors.B: Pulling power destroys volatile RAM evidence - exactly where fileless malware resides.
distractors.D: Copying a few files with OS tools alters metadata, misses memory-resident artifacts, and isn't a sound, verifiable acquisition.

explanation.exam_pattern: Live memory first (fileless), then write-blocked, hash-verified disk image = sound acquisition (order of volatility + integrity).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 4 — Digital forensics (memory/disk acquisition, write blocker, hashing)

questions.stem: A control is being evaluated against a risk whose single loss expectancy is $50,000 and whose annualized rate of occurrence is 2.0 (ALE = $100,000). The proposed control would cut the ARO to 0.5 (ALE = $25,000) but costs $40,000 per year to run. Using cost-benefit analysis, what is the net annual value of deploying the control?

explanation.correct: Value of a safeguard = (ALE before - ALE after) - annual cost of the control = ($100,000 - $25,000) - $40,000 = $75,000 - $40,000 = $35,000 net benefit, so the control is cost-justified.

distractors.A: $25,000 is the residual ALE after the control, not the net value of deploying it.
distractors.B: $60,000 would be ALE-before minus the control cost ($100,000 - $40,000); it ignores the $25,000 of residual ALE that remains.
distractors.D: $75,000 is the gross risk reduction (ALE before - ALE after) before subtracting the $40,000 annual cost of the control.

explanation.exam_pattern: Safeguard value = (ALE_before - ALE_after) - annual control cost; a positive result means the control is cost-justified.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Risk management (cost-benefit analysis, ALE reduction vs safeguard cost)

questions.stem: A startup must assess risk to a brand-new product line for which no historical loss data, asset valuations, or occurrence rates exist. Leadership needs a defensible way to rank risks quickly for a board meeting next week. Which assessment approach is MOST appropriate given these constraints?

options.text: An actuarial Monte Carlo simulation of financial loss distributions
A fully quantitative analysis computing SLE, ARO, and ALE for each risk
A qualitative assessment using a likelihood-versus-impact risk matrix (heat map) with defined rating scales
Skip assessment and accept all risks until data accumulates

explanation.correct: With no reliable numeric data and a short timeline, a qualitative likelihood x impact matrix with agreed rating scales lets stakeholders rank and communicate risks quickly without inventing false precision.

distractors.A: Monte Carlo simulation requires probability distributions derived from data the startup does not have, and is heavier than the timeline allows.
distractors.B: Quantitative analysis needs credible asset values and occurrence rates, which do not exist for a brand-new product line.
distractors.D: Blanket acceptance abdicates risk management and gives the board nothing to decide on.

explanation.exam_pattern: No reliable numeric data + need speed -> qualitative (heat map); quantitative needs defensible $ and ARO figures.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Risk management (qualitative vs quantitative assessment)

questions.stem: A bank evaluates launching a cryptocurrency custody service. Analysis shows the regulatory and security risk exceeds the firm's risk appetite and cannot be sufficiently mitigated at acceptable cost, so leadership decides not to offer the service at all. Which risk-treatment strategy is this?

options.text: Risk transference
Risk avoidance
Risk mitigation
Risk acceptance

explanation.correct: Choosing not to engage in the risky activity at all - eliminating the exposure by not launching the service - is risk avoidance.

distractors.A: Transference shifts financial impact to a third party (e.g., insurance) while still performing the activity.
distractors.C: Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact with controls while still undertaking the activity; the firm instead forgoes it entirely.
distractors.D: Acceptance means proceeding and absorbing the risk; here the firm declines to proceed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Don't do the risky activity at all = avoidance; proceed-with-controls = mitigation; proceed-and-absorb = acceptance; offload loss = transference.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Risk management (risk response: avoidance)

questions.stem: A CISO wants a structured, quantitative model to express cyber risk to executives in financial terms by decomposing it into factors such as loss event frequency and loss magnitude, rather than using ordinal high/medium/low ratings. Which framework is purpose-built for this?

options.text: The Cyber Kill Chain
The MITRE ATT&CK framework
FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk)
The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard

explanation.correct: FAIR is a quantitative risk-analysis model that decomposes risk into loss event frequency and loss magnitude (and their sub-factors), expressing risk as a probable financial loss range for better executive decision-making.

distractors.A: The Cyber Kill Chain models intrusion phases, not financial risk factoring.
distractors.B: MITRE ATT&CK catalogs adversary tactics and techniques; it is not a financial risk-quantification model.
distractors.D: OWASP ASVS defines application security verification requirements, not enterprise risk quantification.

explanation.exam_pattern: Quantify risk in dollars via loss frequency x magnitude = FAIR; ATT&CK/Kill Chain = adversary behavior, not risk math.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Risk management (quantitative risk models, FAIR)

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the three-letter acronym: A metric that acts as an early-warning signal that risk exposure is increasing (for example, a rising percentage of unpatched critical systems trending toward a defined threshold) is called a key risk indicator, abbreviated ______.

explanation.correct: A KRI (key risk indicator) is a forward-looking metric that signals changing risk exposure against a threshold, letting leadership act before a KPI (performance outcome) degrades or a loss occurs.
explanation.exam_pattern: Leading signal that risk is rising = KRI; KPI measures performance/outcome achieved.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Risk management (key risk indicators, risk monitoring)

questions.stem: An enterprise adopting NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 notices it adds a function absent from the original five (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover). Which function did CSF 2.0 add, and what is its purpose?

options.text: Audit - requiring annual third-party certification
Govern - establishing and monitoring the organization's cybersecurity risk-management strategy, expectations, roles, and policy
Encrypt - mandating cryptographic controls for all data
Automate - requiring SOAR for all response actions

explanation.correct: CSF 2.0 (published February 2024) added the Govern function, which sets and oversees the cyber-risk strategy, roles/responsibilities, policy, and oversight that inform the other five functions; it also broadened the framework's scope to all organizations, not just critical infrastructure.

distractors.A: CSF is a voluntary outcome-based framework; it adds no mandatory certification function.
distractors.C: 'Encrypt' is not a CSF function; cryptography appears as outcomes within Protect, not a top-level function.
distractors.D: 'Automate' is not a CSF function; CSF 2.0 added Govern, not an automation mandate.

explanation.exam_pattern: CSF 2.0 = 6 functions; the new one is Govern (strategy/oversight wrapping Identify-Protect-Detect-Respond-Recover).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Compliance frameworks (NIST CSF 2.0, Govern function)

questions.stem: A retailer wants to shrink the cost and scope of its annual PCI DSS assessment. Most of its corporate network never stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, yet it currently sits in the same flat network as the point-of-sale systems. Which action MOST effectively reduces PCI DSS scope?

options.text: Network segmentation that isolates the cardholder data environment (CDE) from out-of-scope systems
Purchase cyber-liability insurance covering card-breach fines
Increase the password length policy company-wide
Encrypt all corporate email

explanation.correct: PCI DSS scope includes all systems in or connected to the cardholder data environment. Effective network segmentation that isolates the CDE removes properly separated systems from scope, reducing assessment effort and cost (segmentation is explicitly recognized by PCI DSS as a scope-reduction method).

distractors.B: Insurance transfers some financial impact but does not reduce the technical assessment scope.
distractors.C: Longer passwords strengthen one control but do not segment the network or reduce the set of in-scope systems.
distractors.D: Encrypting corporate email does not isolate the CDE or remove systems from PCI scope.

explanation.exam_pattern: Shrink PCI DSS scope -> segment/isolate the CDE so unrelated systems are provably out of scope.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Compliance frameworks (PCI DSS scope reduction via segmentation)

questions.stem: A defense contractor must demonstrate it protects Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) to win U.S. Department of Defense contracts, with security requirements drawn from NIST SP 800-171 and verified through tiered, independent assessment. Which program governs this requirement?

options.text: PCI DSS
SOC 2
CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification)
FedRAMP

explanation.correct: CMMC is the DoD program that verifies defense-industrial-base contractors protect CUI (and FCI) using NIST SP 800-171-based requirements, assessed at tiered maturity levels with third-party or government verification.

distractors.A: PCI DSS protects payment-card data, unrelated to DoD CUI.
distractors.B: SOC 2 is a service-organization attestation against the Trust Services Criteria, not the DoD's CUI certification program.
distractors.D: FedRAMP authorizes cloud service providers for federal agency use (NIST SP 800-53), not DIB contractor CUI protection.

explanation.exam_pattern: DoD contractors + CUI + NIST 800-171 + tiered certification = CMMC; FedRAMP = federal cloud authorization (800-53).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Compliance frameworks (CMMC, NIST SP 800-171, CUI)

questions.stem: A U.S. hospital network must comply with the HIPAA Security Rule for electronic protected health information (ePHI). The Security Rule requires safeguards in which three categories?

options.text: Administrative, physical, and technical safeguards
Preventive, detective, and corrective safeguards
Strategic, operational, and tactical safeguards
Confidentiality, integrity, and availability safeguards

explanation.correct: The HIPAA Security Rule organizes required and addressable safeguards for ePHI into three categories: administrative (e.g., risk analysis, workforce training), physical (e.g., facility access), and technical (e.g., access control, audit, encryption).

distractors.B: Preventive/detective/corrective are general control-function types, not the HIPAA Security Rule's safeguard categories.
distractors.C: Strategic/operational/tactical describe planning levels, not HIPAA safeguard categories.
distractors.D: CIA is the security objective triad, not the Security Rule's safeguard structure (though safeguards support CIA).

explanation.exam_pattern: HIPAA Security Rule safeguards = administrative + physical + technical (for ePHI).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Compliance frameworks (HIPAA Security Rule safeguards)

questions.stem: A publicly traded U.S. company must ensure the integrity and accuracy of its financial reporting, including IT general controls over the systems that produce financial statements, with executive sign-off on control effectiveness. Which regulation is the primary driver?

options.text: FERPA
GLBA (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act)
SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley Act)
GDPR

explanation.correct: Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) mandates accurate financial reporting and internal controls over financial reporting for U.S. public companies, including IT general controls, with executive (CEO/CFO) certification of their effectiveness.

distractors.A: FERPA protects the privacy of student education records, unrelated to financial reporting.
distractors.B: GLBA governs the privacy and protection of consumers' financial information at financial institutions, not financial-statement reporting integrity.
distractors.D: GDPR regulates personal data of EU data subjects, not corporate financial reporting controls.

explanation.exam_pattern: Public-company financial-reporting integrity + ITGC + executive certification = SOX.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Compliance frameworks (SOX, IT general controls)

questions.stem: A company wants a single signed document that tells employees what they may and may not do with corporate systems, email, and internet access - and that it can point to when disciplining misuse. Which document BEST fills this need?

options.text: A business impact analysis (BIA)
A disaster recovery plan (DRP)
A service-level agreement (SLA)
An acceptable use policy (AUP)

explanation.correct: An acceptable use policy defines permitted and prohibited use of organizational systems and resources; employees typically acknowledge it, giving the organization a basis to enforce consequences for misuse.

distractors.A: A BIA identifies critical processes and impacts of disruption; it is not a user-conduct policy.
distractors.B: A DRP details how to recover IT after a disaster, not acceptable user behavior.
distractors.C: An SLA sets service performance commitments between parties, not employee usage rules.

explanation.exam_pattern: Rules for how users may use IT resources, signed/acknowledged = AUP.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Governance (acceptable use policy)

questions.stem: A business unit cannot meet a mandatory encryption standard for a legacy system before a hard deadline. Which governance mechanism is the CORRECT way to proceed while maintaining accountability?

options.text: Quietly ignore the standard until the system is retired
Delete the audit finding from the risk register
A formal policy exception/waiver documenting the gap, compensating controls, a remediation timeline, and risk-owner acceptance sign-off
Permanently lower the organization-wide encryption standard so nothing is non-compliant

explanation.correct: A documented exception/waiver records the deviation, the compensating controls reducing interim risk, a remediation plan with dates, and formal risk acceptance by the accountable owner - preserving governance and auditability.

distractors.A: Silently ignoring a standard removes accountability and oversight and likely breaches policy/audit requirements.
distractors.B: Deleting the finding conceals risk and undermines the integrity of the risk register.
distractors.D: Lowering the standard for everyone to mask one system's gap weakens security broadly and is not a targeted, time-bound exception.

explanation.exam_pattern: Can't meet a standard -> formal, time-bound exception with compensating controls + risk-owner sign-off, not silent non-compliance.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Governance (policy exceptions/waivers, risk acceptance)

questions.stem: After selecting a vendor, an organization continues to apply ongoing, reasonable security measures and monitoring expected of a prudent operator to protect the data it is responsible for. Which principle does this ongoing, prudent-person effort represent?

options.text: Due diligence
Separation of duties
Least privilege
Due care

explanation.correct: Due care is the ongoing exercise of reasonable, prudent protection and oversight (the 'prudent person' standard) once a decision is made; due diligence is the up-front investigation that informs the decision.

distractors.A: Due diligence is the prior investigative homework (e.g., vetting the vendor), not the ongoing protective effort afterward.
distractors.B: Separation of duties splits incompatible tasks among people to curb fraud, a different control.
distractors.C: Least privilege limits access rights to the minimum needed, not the standard of ongoing prudent care.

explanation.exam_pattern: Due diligence = investigate before (homework); due care = act prudently/continuously after (the ongoing effort).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Governance (due care vs due diligence)

questions.stem: A bank requires finance employees to take at least five consecutive business days of vacation each year, during which another employee performs their duties. From a controls standpoint, this practice functions primarily as which type of control?

options.text: A detective control that surfaces fraud or errors concealed by ongoing activity
A physical control protecting the facility
A deterrent control that only discourages policy violations
A preventive control that stops fraud from occurring

explanation.correct: Mandatory vacation is chiefly a detective control: when someone else must cover the role, schemes that require the perpetrator's continuous presence to hide (e.g., rolling fraud) tend to surface. It also has deterrent value, but its primary control function is detection.

distractors.B: It is an administrative/personnel control, not a physical one.
distractors.C: Deterrence is a secondary effect; the recognized primary purpose is detecting concealed fraud/errors.
distractors.D: It does not technically prevent fraud from happening; it reveals concealed activity after the fact.

explanation.exam_pattern: Mandatory vacation / job rotation = primarily detective (uncovers hidden fraud), with deterrent side effect.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Governance (personnel controls, control functions)

questions.stem: An auditor asks the security team to classify its controls by the CompTIA control-category model. A security guard at the lobby, a visitor sign-in log, and bollards outside the entrance are BEST categorized as which control category?

options.text: Operational controls
Technical controls
Managerial controls
Physical controls

explanation.correct: Guards, sign-in logs at a physical entrance, and bollards act on the physical environment to protect people and facilities, so they are physical controls (by category). Note a control's category - what it acts on - is distinct from its function (deterrent/preventive/detective/etc.).

distractors.A: Operational controls are processes executed by people (e.g., awareness training, change management), distinct from physical barriers.
distractors.B: Technical (logical) controls are implemented in hardware/software/firmware (e.g., firewalls, encryption), not guards or bollards.
distractors.C: Managerial controls are administrative/policy and risk-management activities (policies, risk assessments), not physical barriers.

explanation.exam_pattern: Category = what the control acts on: managerial (policy), operational (people/process), technical (tech), physical (world).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Governance (control categories: managerial/operational/technical/physical)

questions.stem: A company and a strategic supplier expect many projects over several years. They want to negotiate overarching legal terms (liability, IP, security requirements, confidentiality) ONCE, then define each project's specific deliverables, timelines, and prices in separate, lightweight documents. Which pairing of agreement types BEST fits?

options.text: A master service agreement (MSA) for the overarching terms, with per-project statements of work (SOWs)
A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) for the overarching terms, with per-project MOUs
A service-level agreement (SLA) for the overarching terms, with per-project NDAs
A business partnership agreement (BPA) for the overarching terms, with per-project SLAs

explanation.correct: An MSA establishes the master legal/commercial terms that govern the whole relationship, while each engagement's specific scope, deliverables, schedule, and price are captured in a statement of work (SOW) that references the MSA - exactly the negotiate-once, execute-many pattern.

distractors.B: An NDA only covers confidentiality, not the full commercial terms; an MOU is typically non-binding intent, not enforceable deliverables.
distractors.C: An SLA defines service-performance metrics, not the master legal framework; NDAs do not define deliverables.
distractors.D: A BPA governs a partnership's profit/responsibility sharing; SLAs define performance metrics, not per-project deliverables/scope.

explanation.exam_pattern: Negotiate master terms once (MSA) + define each project's scope/deliverables (SOW).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Third-party risk (agreement types: MSA, SOW)

questions.stem: After a software supplier's build system was compromised and shipped a trojanized update to customers, a security team wants assurance that future vendor artifacts are authentic and built from the expected source with a tamper-evident record of how they were produced. Which combination BEST addresses this supply-chain integrity goal?

options.text: Require the vendor to carry more cyber-insurance
Verify code-signing signatures on artifacts plus build provenance/attestations (e.g., SLSA) and an SBOM for each release
Scan the vendor's public website with a vulnerability scanner
Rely on the vendor's marketing claims of security

explanation.correct: Authenticity and build integrity come from verifying code-signing signatures, consuming signed build provenance/attestations (e.g., the SLSA framework) that prove what source and pipeline produced the artifact, and reviewing an SBOM - together making tampering detectable.

distractors.A: Insurance transfers some financial loss but does nothing to verify artifact authenticity or build provenance.
distractors.C: Scanning the website does not attest to how shipped software artifacts were built or whether they were tampered with.
distractors.D: Marketing claims are not verifiable assurance of artifact integrity.

explanation.exam_pattern: Trojanized-update/build compromise -> code signing + build provenance/attestation (SLSA) + SBOM to verify authenticity and integrity.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Third-party/supply-chain risk (code signing, build provenance/SLSA, SBOM)

questions.stem: Before signing with a SaaS vendor, legal and security want to ensure the company can retrieve its data in a usable, standard format and migrate away if the vendor fails, raises prices, or is acquired - avoiding being trapped. Which contractual consideration MOST directly addresses this?

options.text: A data portability and exit (off-boarding) strategy addressing vendor lock-in
A right-to-audit clause
A uptime service-level agreement
A mutual non-disclosure agreement

explanation.correct: Defining data portability (export in standard formats), transition assistance, and an exit strategy up front mitigates vendor lock-in, so the organization can move providers or bring the service in-house without being held hostage.

distractors.B: A right-to-audit clause enables inspecting the vendor's controls, but does not ensure data retrievability or a clean exit.
distractors.C: An uptime SLA governs availability performance, not the ability to exit and take your data.
distractors.D: An NDA protects confidentiality; it does not guarantee data portability or migration.

explanation.exam_pattern: Avoid being trapped by a vendor -> plan data portability + exit strategy (lock-in mitigation) before signing.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Third-party risk (vendor lock-in, data portability, exit strategy)

questions.stem: A vendor announces that a widely used appliance has reached end-of-service-life (EOSL): no more security patches will ever be released, but the business still depends on it. Which statement BEST captures the risk and the appropriate governance response?

options.text: The appliance becomes more secure after EOSL because attackers lose interest
EOSL is purely a budgeting concern with no security impact
Newly discovered vulnerabilities will go unpatched forever, so the organization must plan replacement and, in the interim, isolate/compensate and formally accept the residual risk
A support contract renewal will automatically restore patches

explanation.correct: After EOSL the vendor issues no further security fixes, so any new vulnerability is permanently exposed. Governance requires a replacement/migration plan and, until then, compensating controls (isolation, monitoring, restricted access) with documented risk acceptance.

distractors.A: Lack of patches makes systems more vulnerable over time; attacker interest in widely deployed legacy gear often rises.
distractors.B: Unpatched, internet-reachable or critical systems carry real and growing security risk, not just cost.
distractors.D: EOSL means support/patching has ended; renewal is generally unavailable or does not restore security updates.

explanation.exam_pattern: EOL/EOSL = no more patches -> plan replacement + isolate/compensate + formal risk acceptance in the interim.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Third-party risk (end-of-life/EOSL unsupported software)

questions.stem: A manufacturer of safety-critical hardware is worried about counterfeit or tampered components entering its product through the hardware supply chain. Which TWO controls MOST directly reduce hardware supply-chain tampering/counterfeiting risk? (Choose two.)

options.text: Buy the cheapest components available on open gray markets to cut costs
Disable all logging on the manufacturing line to improve throughput
Validate device integrity with hardware roots of trust and signed/attested firmware before deployment
Source components only through authorized/trusted suppliers and verify provenance (anti-counterfeit authentication, tamper-evident packaging)

explanation.correct: Buying from authorized suppliers with verified provenance and tamper-evident controls reduces the chance counterfeit/tampered parts enter, and validating integrity via hardware roots of trust and signed/attested firmware detects tampering before devices are trusted and deployed.

distractors.A: Gray-market sourcing is a primary vector for counterfeit and tampered components - it increases risk.
distractors.B: Disabling manufacturing-line logging removes the visibility needed to detect and investigate tampering.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hardware supply chain -> trusted/authorized sourcing + provenance/tamper-evidence + hardware root-of-trust/firmware attestation.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Third-party/supply-chain risk (hardware provenance, counterfeit, root of trust)

questions.stem: An organization is rolling out a four-tier data classification scheme (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted). When a new dataset is created, who is responsible for assigning its classification level?

options.text: The end users who read the data
The external auditor
The data custodian who runs the storage systems
The data owner (the accountable business leader for that data)

explanation.correct: The data owner - the senior/business role accountable for a data asset - determines its classification and the protection requirements; custodians then implement the controls that the classification demands.

distractors.A: End users consume data within granted permissions; they do not assign classification.
distractors.B: Auditors assess whether classification and controls are applied correctly; they do not own or assign the classification.
distractors.C: The custodian maintains and protects the data per the owner's direction (implements backups, access, encryption) but does not set the classification.

explanation.exam_pattern: Owner (accountable) classifies and sets requirements; custodian (hands-on) implements protection.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Data governance (classification, data owner responsibilities)

questions.stem: A research team wants to analyze customer datasets while reducing privacy risk. In Technique X, direct identifiers are replaced with reversible tokens so records can be re-linked via a separately held key; in Technique Y, identifiers are irreversibly removed so individuals can no longer be re-identified. Under GDPR, which statement is correct?

options.text: Both are anonymization and both fall outside GDPR
Technique X is anonymization and falls outside GDPR; Technique Y is pseudonymization and remains personal data
Both are pseudonymization and both fall outside GDPR
Technique X is pseudonymization and remains personal data under GDPR; Technique Y is anonymization and, if truly irreversible, falls outside GDPR's scope

explanation.correct: Reversible replacement with a separately held key is pseudonymization; because re-identification is still possible, GDPR treats pseudonymized data as personal data. Truly irreversible anonymization removes the ability to re-identify, so genuinely anonymized data is outside GDPR's scope.

distractors.A: Reversible tokenization keyed to a secret is pseudonymization and stays in scope; it is not anonymization.
distractors.B: This reverses the definitions - reversible-with-key is pseudonymization, not anonymization.
distractors.C: Irreversible removal is anonymization, not pseudonymization; the two differ in reversibility and legal scope.

explanation.exam_pattern: Pseudonymization = reversible (keyed) -> still personal data under GDPR; anonymization = irreversible -> outside GDPR (if truly non-re-identifiable).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Data governance (pseudonymization vs anonymization, GDPR)

questions.stem: In a data-governance RACI, one role is accountable for data quality, definitions, and appropriate use within a business domain - acting as the liaison between business and IT - without necessarily owning or operating the storage. Which role is this?

options.text: Data processor
Data custodian
Data steward
Data subject

explanation.correct: A data steward manages data quality, metadata/definitions, and appropriate use within a domain, bridging business and technical teams and enforcing the owner's policies day to day.

distractors.A: A processor (GDPR) processes personal data on a controller's behalf - a legal/privacy role, not internal data-quality stewardship.
distractors.B: A custodian provides technical safekeeping (storage, backups, access enforcement), not business-level quality/definition stewardship.
distractors.D: A data subject is the individual the personal data is about, not a governance role.

explanation.exam_pattern: Steward = data quality/definitions/appropriate-use liaison; custodian = technical safekeeping; owner = accountable classifier.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Data governance (data roles: steward vs custodian)

questions.stem: A retention schedule requires that customer records be irrecoverably destroyed at end of life. The data is spread across multi-tenant cloud storage and SSDs where physical destruction and reliable overwriting are impractical. Which method BEST assures the data is rendered unrecoverable?

options.text: Crypto-shredding: encrypt the data at rest and then securely destroy the encryption keys so the ciphertext is unrecoverable
Move the records to an archive bucket and delete the index
A single-pass overwrite of the logical file
Degauss the cloud provider's drives

explanation.correct: Crypto-shredding (cryptographic erasure) destroys the keys that decrypt the data, so the remaining ciphertext is computationally unrecoverable - ideal where physical destruction, degaussing, or reliable overwrite are impractical (SSD wear-leveling, multi-tenant cloud).

distractors.B: Deleting an index leaves the underlying data recoverable; it is not secure destruction.
distractors.C: SSD wear-leveling and over-provisioning mean a single logical overwrite may not touch all physical cells, so data can persist.
distractors.D: Degaussing applies to magnetic media and is not an option you can perform on a cloud provider's drives (and is ineffective on SSDs).

explanation.exam_pattern: Cloud/SSD secure destruction when physical/overwrite is impractical = crypto-shredding (destroy the keys).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Data governance (retention/disposal, cryptographic erasure)

questions.stem: A European subsidiary needs to transfer EU residents' personal data to its U.S.-based parent for processing. Following the invalidation of a prior framework (Schrems II), which mechanism do organizations MOST commonly rely on to legitimize such cross-border transfers, often paired with a transfer impact assessment and supplementary safeguards?

options.text: A service-level agreement (SLA)
A software bill of materials (SBOM)
A non-disclosure agreement (NDA)
Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)

explanation.correct: Standard Contractual Clauses are EU-approved contractual terms that provide a lawful basis for transferring personal data to third countries; after Schrems II, organizations commonly use SCCs together with a transfer impact assessment and supplementary technical/organizational safeguards (adequacy decisions or BCRs are alternatives).

distractors.A: An SLA sets service-performance commitments, not a lawful basis for cross-border personal-data transfer.
distractors.B: An SBOM is a software component inventory, unrelated to data-transfer legality.
distractors.C: An NDA protects confidentiality between parties but is not a recognized GDPR cross-border transfer mechanism.

explanation.exam_pattern: EU-to-third-country transfer, post-Schrems II -> SCCs (+ transfer impact assessment/safeguards); adequacy decision or BCRs as alternatives.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 1 — Data governance (cross-border transfers, SCCs, data sovereignty)

questions.stem: An application must encrypt large files and deliver them to many recipients efficiently, giving each recipient the ability to decrypt without sharing a secret key out-of-band. Which cryptographic design BEST meets both the performance and key-distribution needs?

options.text: A hybrid cryptosystem: encrypt the file with a random symmetric key (e.g., AES), then encrypt that symmetric key to each recipient's public key
Encrypt the entire file separately with each recipient's RSA public key
Publish a SHA-256 hash of the file to each recipient
Encrypt the file once with a single shared symmetric key manually distributed to all recipients

explanation.correct: Hybrid encryption uses fast symmetric crypto for the bulk data and asymmetric crypto only to wrap the small symmetric key for each recipient - combining symmetric speed with asymmetric key distribution (no out-of-band secret sharing).

distractors.B: Asymmetric encryption is slow and size-limited; encrypting large files directly with RSA per recipient is impractical and inefficient.
distractors.C: A hash provides integrity verification, not confidentiality - it does not encrypt the file.
distractors.D: A single manually distributed shared key creates the classic key-distribution/revocation problem and risks exposure to all if leaked.

explanation.exam_pattern: Bulk data + multiple recipients -> hybrid: symmetric key encrypts data, asymmetric wraps the key per recipient.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Cryptography (hybrid cryptosystem, symmetric vs asymmetric roles)

questions.stem: A developer needs a single symmetric cipher mode that provides BOTH confidentiality and built-in integrity/authenticity (authenticated encryption), so a tampered ciphertext is detected on decryption without bolting on a separate MAC. Which choice is BEST?

options.text: AES in CBC mode with no additional MAC
AES in ECB mode
AES in CTR mode with no additional MAC
AES in GCM mode (an AEAD mode)

explanation.correct: AES-GCM is an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data) mode: it provides confidentiality and an integrity/authenticity tag in one construction, so tampering is detected on decryption.

distractors.A: CBC alone provides confidentiality but no integrity; without a MAC it is vulnerable to tampering/padding-oracle attacks.
distractors.B: ECB provides neither integrity nor good confidentiality - identical plaintext blocks yield identical ciphertext, leaking structure.
distractors.C: CTR alone is a confidentiality-only stream mode; without a MAC it offers no integrity/authenticity.

explanation.exam_pattern: Confidentiality + integrity in one mode = AEAD (AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305); CBC/CTR need a separate MAC; ECB is unsafe.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Cryptography (cipher modes, authenticated encryption/AEAD)

questions.stem: A review finds that an application encrypts structured records with AES in ECB mode. The security engineer flags it as unsafe. What is the PRIMARY weakness of ECB that justifies this?

options.text: ECB automatically transmits the key with the ciphertext
Identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks, revealing patterns/structure in the data
ECB can only encrypt data smaller than one block
ECB uses keys that are too long, slowing performance

explanation.correct: ECB encrypts each block independently with no IV/chaining, so identical plaintext blocks map to identical ciphertext blocks - leaking patterns (the classic 'ECB penguin'). Use a chaining/AEAD mode with a unique IV/nonce instead.

distractors.A: ECB does not transmit the key; keys are never embedded by the mode.
distractors.C: ECB handles data of many blocks; its problem is per-block determinism, not a size limit.
distractors.D: Key length is unrelated to ECB's weakness; the flaw is deterministic block mapping, not key size.

explanation.exam_pattern: ECB leaks structure (same plaintext block -> same ciphertext block); prefer AEAD/chaining modes with unique IV/nonce.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Cryptography (ECB weakness, cipher modes)

questions.stem: A recipient must be able to verify that a message truly came from the claimed sender, was not altered, and that the sender cannot later deny sending it. Which mechanism provides all three (authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation)?

options.text: A digital signature: the sender signs a hash of the message with their private key, and anyone verifies it with the sender's public key
Symmetric encryption of the message with a shared key
Encrypting the message with the sender's public key
An HMAC computed with a key shared between sender and recipient

explanation.correct: A digital signature (sign the message hash with the sender's private key; verify with the sender's public key) proves authenticity and integrity and provides non-repudiation, since only the holder of the private key could have produced it.

distractors.B: Symmetric encryption with a shared key provides confidentiality (and some integrity with AEAD) but no non-repudiation - the key is shared.
distractors.C: Encrypting with the sender's public key is nonsensical for authentication - anyone has that public key, and only the sender's private key could decrypt, providing confidentiality to the sender, not a signature.
distractors.D: HMAC gives integrity and authentication but NOT non-repudiation, because both parties share the same secret key and either could have produced it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Authentication + integrity + non-repudiation = digital signature (sign hash with private key). Shared-secret schemes (HMAC/symmetric) give no non-repudiation.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Cryptography (digital signatures, non-repudiation)

questions.stem: Two internal services share a secret key and need a fast way to verify that messages between them are authentic and unmodified. Non-repudiation to outside third parties is explicitly NOT required. Which mechanism is the BEST fit for these constraints?

options.text: A CRC32 checksum appended to each message
Base64 encoding of each message
An HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) using the shared secret
RSA digital signatures on every message

explanation.correct: HMAC uses a shared secret with a hash function to provide fast integrity and authenticity between parties that already share the key - appropriate when non-repudiation is not needed and signature overhead is undesirable.

distractors.A: CRC32 detects accidental transmission errors but is not cryptographic - an attacker can forge messages with matching CRCs.
distractors.B: Base64 is encoding, providing neither integrity nor authenticity.
distractors.D: Digital signatures add non-repudiation and public-key overhead that the scenario explicitly does not need, making them heavier than required.

explanation.exam_pattern: Shared secret + integrity/authenticity, no non-repudiation needed = HMAC; need non-repudiation -> digital signature.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Cryptography (HMAC vs digital signatures)

questions.stem: A security engineer is selecting NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms to replace RSA/ECDSA digital signatures. They want a primary lattice-based signature algorithm plus a conservative hash-based alternative as a backup in case the lattice assumption is weakened. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Primary: ML-DSA (FIPS 204); backup: SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, hash-based)
Primary: SHA-3; backup: HMAC-SHA-256
Primary: ML-KEM (FIPS 203); backup: AES-256
Primary: RSA-4096; backup: ECDSA P-384

explanation.correct: ML-DSA (FIPS 204, from CRYSTALS-Dilithium) is NIST's primary post-quantum signature standard; SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, from SPHINCS+) is a stateless hash-based signature standard used as a conservative backup that does not rely on lattice assumptions.

distractors.B: SHA-3 and HMAC are hashing/MAC primitives, not digital-signature algorithms.
distractors.C: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is a key-encapsulation mechanism for key exchange, not a signature algorithm; AES-256 is symmetric encryption, not a signature.
distractors.D: RSA-4096 and ECDSA are classical algorithms broken by Shor's algorithm on a large quantum computer - the very thing being replaced.

explanation.exam_pattern: PQC signatures: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) primary (lattice) + SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) hash-based backup; ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is for key exchange.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Cryptography (post-quantum signatures: FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA)

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Designing systems so that cryptographic algorithms and key sizes can be swapped out with minimal disruption - essential for migrating to post-quantum algorithms - is known as cryptographic ______.

explanation.correct: Cryptographic agility is the ability to replace algorithms, parameters, and keys with minimal code/architecture disruption, letting an organization respond quickly as algorithms are deprecated or broken (central to post-quantum migration).
explanation.exam_pattern: Swap crypto algorithms/keys with minimal disruption = crypto-agility (key enabler of PQC migration).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Cryptography (crypto-agility)

questions.stem: An administrator is requesting a TLS certificate from an internal CA for a new web server. Which statement correctly describes the certificate-signing request (CSR) process and key handling?

options.text: The administrator sends the server's private key to the CA so the CA can sign it
The administrator creates a self-signed certificate and the CA simply counts it as trusted

The server generates a key pair locally; the CSR contains the public key and identity and is signed by the matching private key, which never leaves the server; the CA validates and issues the certificate
The CA generates the server's private key and emails it to the administrator

explanation.correct: The requester generates the key pair locally, builds a CSR containing the public key and subject identity (proving possession by signing it with the private key), and submits it; the CA validates and issues the signed certificate. The private key never leaves the server.

distractors.A: Private keys must never be sent to the CA - only the public key (in the CSR) is shared.
distractors.B: A self-signed certificate is not CA-validated trust; the CA must actually sign the CSR for the certificate to chain to the CA.
distractors.D: A CA generating and emailing private keys defeats key confidentiality; private keys should be generated and kept by the owner.

explanation.exam_pattern: CSR carries the PUBLIC key + identity; the private key stays with the requester; the CA validates and signs.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — PKI (certificate enrollment, CSR, key handling)

questions.stem: A mobile banking app wants to ensure it will only trust its own backend's specific certificate/public key, so that a fraudulently issued certificate from ANY otherwise-trusted CA cannot enable a man-in-the-middle attack. Which technique achieves this, and what is its main operational trade-off?

options.text: OCSP stapling; the trade-off is higher CA load
Certificate (public-key) pinning; the trade-off is that routine certificate rotation/renewal breaks the app unless pins are updated and managed carefully
Using a wildcard certificate; the trade-off is weaker encryption
Enabling HSTS; the trade-off is slower TLS handshakes

explanation.correct: Certificate/public-key pinning hard-codes trust in a specific cert or key, so even a rogue certificate from a trusted CA is rejected - defeating many MITM scenarios. The trade-off is operational brittleness: when the legitimate certificate/key is rotated, the pins must be updated or clients break.

distractors.A: OCSP stapling conveys revocation status efficiently; it does not restrict trust to a specific pinned certificate.
distractors.C: A wildcard certificate covers subdomains; it does not pin trust and does not weaken the encryption strength.
distractors.D: HSTS forces HTTPS and prevents downgrade, but does not pin a specific certificate/key.

explanation.exam_pattern: Trust only our specific cert/key (defeat rogue-CA MITM) = pinning; cost = brittle on rotation/renewal.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — PKI (certificate pinning, trade-offs)

questions.stem: An enterprise encrypts employee laptops and files with per-user keys. Management requires the ability to recover encrypted business data if an employee leaves abruptly or loses their key. Which PKI capability provides this while keeping keys protected?

options.text: Shortening certificate validity periods
Perfect forward secrecy on all sessions
Key escrow with a designated recovery agent (securely storing a protected copy of the decryption key)
Certificate pinning in the email client

explanation.correct: Key escrow stores a protected copy of decryption keys (or uses a key-recovery agent) so the organization can recover encrypted data when a user is unavailable or a key is lost - balanced with strict controls (e.g., M-of-N) to prevent abuse.

distractors.A: Shorter validity periods limit exposure of certificates but do not enable recovery of encrypted data.
distractors.B: Perfect forward secrecy deliberately prevents recovery of past session keys - the opposite of a data-recovery capability.
distractors.D: Certificate pinning restricts which certificate is trusted; it does not recover lost decryption keys.

explanation.exam_pattern: Recover encrypted data when a key/user is lost = key escrow / recovery agent (guard with split-knowledge/M-of-N).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — PKI (key escrow, key recovery)

questions.stem: A domain owner wants to detect whether ANY certificate authority has mis-issued a certificate for its domains (for example, a rogue or compromised CA issuing a cert the owner never requested). Which mechanism is designed to make such mis-issuance publicly detectable?

options.text: The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)
A certificate revocation list (CRL)
HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)
Certificate Transparency (CT) logs, which publicly record issued certificates for monitoring

explanation.correct: Certificate Transparency requires CAs to publish issued certificates to public, append-only logs; domain owners (and monitors) watch these logs to detect certificates issued for their domains that they never requested, exposing mis-issuance.

distractors.A: OCSP checks the revocation status of a given certificate; it does not enumerate or surface unexpected issuances.
distractors.B: A CRL lists already-revoked certificates; it does not proactively reveal that an unauthorized certificate was issued.
distractors.C: HSTS forces browsers to use HTTPS; it does not detect certificate mis-issuance.

explanation.exam_pattern: Detect rogue/mis-issued certs for your domain = Certificate Transparency (public append-only logs + monitoring).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — PKI (Certificate Transparency, mis-issuance detection)

questions.stem: A software company distributes a desktop application and wants users' systems to verify that the installer genuinely came from the company and has not been modified since it was built. Which type of certificate is purpose-built for this?

options.text: A client authentication certificate
A TLS/SSL server certificate
A code-signing certificate
An S/MIME email certificate

explanation.correct: A code-signing certificate lets the publisher digitally sign executables/installers; the OS or installer verifies the signature to confirm publisher identity and that the binary was not tampered with after signing.

distractors.A: A client authentication certificate proves a client's identity to a server, not the integrity/authorship of distributed software.
distractors.B: A TLS server certificate authenticates a web server for an encrypted session; it does not sign distributed software.
distractors.D: An S/MIME certificate signs/encrypts email, not software binaries.

explanation.exam_pattern: Verify software publisher + integrity of a binary = code-signing certificate.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — PKI (code-signing certificates)

questions.stem: An architect must choose between a single wildcard certificate (*.example.com) and a multi-SAN certificate listing specific hostnames, to secure many subdomains. Which statement accurately captures the security trade-off?

options.text: A SAN certificate cannot be used for more than one hostname
A wildcard certificate encrypts more strongly than a SAN certificate

A wildcard covers all first-level subdomains with one key, but compromise of that single private key exposes every subdomain; a multi-SAN certificate explicitly lists names, limiting blast radius but requiring reissuance to add names
Wildcard certificates cannot be revoked

explanation.correct: A wildcard is convenient - one certificate/key secures all first-level subdomains - but that shared private key becomes a single point of compromise affecting every subdomain. A multi-SAN certificate names each host explicitly, containing exposure, at the cost of reissuing when hostnames change.

distractors.A: SAN (subject alternative name) certificates are specifically designed to cover multiple hostnames.
distractors.B: Encryption strength depends on the key/cipher, not whether the certificate is wildcard or SAN.
distractors.D: Wildcard certificates can be revoked like any other certificate.

explanation.exam_pattern: Wildcard = convenience but one key, broad blast radius; multi-SAN = explicit names, contained exposure, reissue to change.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — PKI (wildcard vs SAN certificates, blast radius)

questions.stem: A stateless REST API authenticates requests with JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). Which practice is MOST critical to prevent token forgery and privilege abuse?

options.text: Store the signing secret in the client application for convenience
Issue long-lived tokens with no expiration to reduce re-authentication
Trust the algorithm specified in the token's own header so clients can choose what they prefer
Verify the token's signature with the expected algorithm/key, reject 'alg: none' and algorithm-confusion, and validate issuer, audience, and expiration claims server-side

explanation.correct: The server must cryptographically verify the JWT signature using the algorithm/key it expects (never honoring attacker-controlled 'alg: none' or RS/HS confusion) and validate iss/aud/exp (and scopes) - otherwise tokens can be forged or misused.

distractors.A: Placing the signing secret in the client exposes it, letting anyone mint valid tokens.
distractors.B: Non-expiring tokens cannot be revoked by expiry and greatly extend the window of abuse if stolen.
distractors.C: Trusting the token's own 'alg' header enables 'alg: none' and algorithm-confusion forgery; the server must pin the expected algorithm.

explanation.exam_pattern: JWT security = verify signature with expected alg/key, reject alg:none, validate iss/aud/exp, short lifetimes, protect signing keys.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Secure integration (JWT/token validation, API authentication)

questions.stem: A SaaS platform sends event notifications to customers' public webhook URLs. A customer wants to be sure an incoming webhook genuinely originated from the SaaS platform and was not forged or replayed by an attacker who found the URL. Which approach does the platform MOST commonly provide for this?

options.text: Check that the request came over HTTP
Rely on the secrecy of the webhook URL alone
Sign each payload with an HMAC using a shared secret (plus a timestamp/nonce); the receiver recomputes and compares the signature and rejects stale timestamps
Trust any request whose body matches the expected JSON schema

explanation.correct: The sender computes an HMAC of the payload (and a timestamp/nonce) with a shared secret and includes it in a header; the receiver recomputes the HMAC to verify authenticity/integrity and rejects stale or replayed timestamps - proving the webhook is genuine.

distractors.A: Plain HTTP offers no authentication and exposes traffic; it does not prove origin.
distractors.B: A 'secret URL' is easily leaked (logs, referrers) and provides no cryptographic authenticity or replay protection.
distractors.D: Matching a schema only checks shape; an attacker can craft well-formed JSON, so it proves nothing about origin.

explanation.exam_pattern: Verify webhook authenticity/integrity = HMAC-signed payload + timestamp/nonce for replay protection; not URL secrecy or schema shape.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Secure integration (webhook security, HMAC signatures)

questions.stem: In a microservices platform, dozens of services call each other's APIs. Security wants to eliminate long-lived static API keys embedded in config and reduce the damage if one service is compromised. Which approach BEST secures this service-to-service (machine) authentication?

options.text: Give every service the same shared static API key stored in a config file
Hard-code credentials into each container image
Issue each workload a short-lived, automatically rotated identity/credential (e.g., mTLS certificates or signed service tokens from an identity provider) scoped with least privilege
Allow unauthenticated internal calls since they are behind the firewall

explanation.correct: Short-lived, automatically rotated workload identities (mTLS certificates or signed service tokens) scoped to least privilege limit the window and blast radius if a service is compromised, and remove brittle static secrets from configuration.

distractors.A: A shared static key means a single leak compromises everything and cannot distinguish or revoke individual services.
distractors.B: Hard-coded image credentials are easily extracted from images/registries and are hard to rotate.
distractors.D: Implicit trust of internal traffic violates zero trust and enables free lateral movement after any foothold.

explanation.exam_pattern: Service-to-service auth -> short-lived, rotated workload identities (mTLS/signed tokens), least privilege; avoid static shared/hard-coded keys.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Secure integration (machine/workload identity, secrets management)

questions.stem: An API aggregates data submitted by multiple partners and passes fields into backend queries and downstream services. To prevent injection and malformed-data attacks across this integration, which control is MOST fundamental at the API boundary?

options.text: Increasing the API's rate limit
Relying on the partner's client-side JavaScript validation
Returning verbose stack traces to help partners debug
Rigorous server-side input validation (allowlist/schema validation, type/length/range checks) with proper output encoding/parameterization downstream

explanation.correct: Never trust external input: enforce strict server-side validation (allowlist/schema, type, length, range) and use parameterization/encoding when passing data to queries or downstream systems - the foundational defense against injection across integrations.

distractors.A: Rate limiting mitigates abuse/DoS but does not stop malicious content in otherwise-allowed requests.
distractors.B: Client-side validation is easily bypassed and cannot be trusted as a security control.
distractors.C: Verbose stack traces leak internal details to attackers and aid exploitation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Integration boundary against injection = server-side allowlist/schema validation + parameterization/encoding; client-side checks are not security.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Secure integration (input validation at API boundaries)

questions.stem: A message travels through several intermediaries (API gateways, message brokers) before reaching its destination, and it must remain confidential and integrity-protected end to end - not readable or alterable by any intermediary. Transport-layer TLS alone is insufficient here. Which approach BEST meets the requirement?

options.text: Compress the message before sending
Apply message-level security: sign and encrypt the payload itself (e.g., JWS/JWE or WS-Security) so protection persists across every intermediary
Encode the message in Base64
Enable TLS 1.3 on each hop and consider it end-to-end

explanation.correct: TLS protects each transport hop but is terminated and re-originated at every intermediary, which can read/alter the plaintext. Message-level security encrypts and signs the payload itself (JWS/JWE, WS-Security), so confidentiality and integrity persist end to end regardless of the intermediaries.

distractors.A: Compression affects size, not confidentiality or integrity.
distractors.C: Base64 is reversible encoding and provides no protection.
distractors.D: Hop-by-hop TLS leaves the message in plaintext at each intermediary where TLS terminates - not true end-to-end protection.

explanation.exam_pattern: Protection must survive intermediaries -> message-level (payload) encryption/signing, not just transport TLS (which is hop-by-hop).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Secure integration (message-level vs transport-level security)

questions.stem: A zero-trust program wants a remote server to cryptographically verify that a laptop booted only trusted, unmodified firmware and OS components before granting it access to sensitive resources. Which capability BEST provides this remote attestation of boot integrity?

options.text: Measured boot, where each boot component is hashed into the TPM's platform configuration registers (PCRs) and the signed measurements are sent to a verifier for remote attestation
A host-based firewall rule set
UEFI Secure Boot alone, which blocks unsigned bootloaders locally
BIOS password protection

explanation.correct: Measured boot records cryptographic hashes of each boot stage into TPM PCRs; the TPM can produce a signed quote of these measurements that a remote verifier evaluates (remote attestation) to confirm the platform booted a known-good state.

distractors.B: A host firewall controls network traffic; it does not attest to boot integrity.
distractors.C: Secure Boot enforces signature checks locally and blocks unsigned components, but by itself it does not produce signed measurements for a remote verifier to attest to.
distractors.D: A BIOS password restricts local configuration access but provides no cryptographic boot attestation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Remote proof of boot integrity = measured boot (TPM PCRs) + remote attestation; Secure Boot = local enforcement of signed components.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Endpoint security (measured boot vs Secure Boot, TPM attestation)

questions.stem: A hardened server must alert the SOC whenever critical system binaries or configuration files are modified, since attackers often tamper with these for persistence. Which control MOST directly detects such unauthorized changes?

options.text: A faster CPU to process logs
A longer password policy for administrators
Disabling the system's audit logs to reduce noise
File integrity monitoring (FIM) that baselines cryptographic hashes and alerts on deviations

explanation.correct: File integrity monitoring establishes a trusted baseline (hashes/attributes) of critical files and alerts when they change unexpectedly, surfacing tampering, rootkits, or unauthorized configuration changes.

distractors.A: CPU speed does not detect file changes.
distractors.B: Stronger passwords reduce credential compromise but do not detect modifications to files.
distractors.C: Disabling audit logs removes evidence and visibility - the opposite of detection.

explanation.exam_pattern: Detect unauthorized changes to critical files/config = FIM (baseline hashes + alert on deviation).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Endpoint security (file integrity monitoring)

questions.stem: A company allows BYOD smartphones to access corporate email and apps. Security must keep corporate data separate from personal data and be able to remove ONLY corporate data if the employee leaves or the device is lost, without wiping the user's personal photos. Which approach BEST achieves this?

options.text: Full-device wipe on any policy violation
Ask employees to manually delete corporate data when they leave
MDM/UEM containerization that isolates managed corporate apps/data and supports selective (corporate-only) wipe
Block all mobile access to corporate resources

explanation.correct: Containerization (via MDM/UEM) separates managed corporate apps and data from personal content and enables a selective wipe that removes only the corporate container - balancing security with employee privacy on BYOD devices.

distractors.A: A full-device wipe destroys personal data, raising privacy and legal concerns on BYOD.
distractors.B: Relying on manual user deletion is unenforceable and unreliable.
distractors.D: Blocking all mobile access defeats the BYOD goal and is more restrictive than needed.

explanation.exam_pattern: BYOD data separation + remove only corporate data = MDM/UEM containerization with selective wipe.

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Endpoint security (MDM/UEM, BYOD containerization, selective wipe)

questions.stem: Analysis shows that most malware and ransomware damage on workstations is amplified because users run with standing local administrator rights. Which control MOST directly reduces this blast radius while still allowing occasional legitimate elevation?

options.text: Remove standing local-admin rights and use endpoint privilege management to broker just-in-time, approved elevation for specific tasks (least privilege)
Allow local admin but require a longer password
Give users two admin accounts instead of one
Install signature antivirus and nothing else

explanation.correct: Removing standing local admin and brokering just-in-time, task-scoped elevation (endpoint privilege management) enforces least privilege, so malware running as the user cannot trivially gain full control of the host.

distractors.B: A longer password does not reduce the privileges malware inherits when the user already has standing admin rights.
distractors.C: A second admin account still leaves standing privileges available to malware running in the user's session.
distractors.D: Signature AV alone misses novel/fileless threats and does not address excessive standing privilege.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reduce malware blast radius on endpoints = remove standing local admin + just-in-time least-privilege elevation (EPM).

references: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 Objectives: Domain 3 — Endpoint security (least privilege, endpoint privilege management)

questions.stem: To protect data on laptops that are frequently lost or stolen, a company wants full-disk encryption whose key cannot be trivially extracted and that resists offline attacks if the drive is removed. Which configuration is STRONGEST?

options.text: Full-disk encryption with the key sealed to the TPM and a required pre-boot authentication factor (PIN/password)
Full-disk encryption with the key stored in a plaintext file on the same disk
Relying on the operating-system login password with no disk encryption
Encrypting only the Documents folder

explanation.correct: Sealing the FDE key to the TPM binds it to the specific platform and keeps it out of general storage, while a pre-boot PIN/password adds a factor so a stolen drive (or a device powered off) cannot be decrypted by simply removing the disk or capturing the key.

distractors.B: Storing the key in plaintext on the same disk defeats the encryption - an attacker reads the key and decrypts.
distractors.C: An OS login password without disk encryption is bypassed by booting another OS or removing the drive.
distractors.D: Encrypting one folder leaves the OS, temp files, and other data exposed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Strong laptop data-at-rest protection = FDE + TPM-sealed key + pre-boot auth (resists drive removal/offline attack).
